title: Rename Columns
statement:
LeetCode poses this one in pandas, on a DataFrame named `students`; here the DataFrame is a table and you answer with one MySQL query.

- `students(id, first, last, age)`: one row per student. `id` and `age` are integers and are never null; `first` and `last` hold the first and last name as text.

Return every row of `students` with its values untouched but its columns renamed, in this order:

- `id` becomes `student_id`
- `first` becomes `first_name`
- `last` becomes `last_name`
- `age` becomes `age_in_years`

No row is added, removed or merged. Rows may come in any order.
constraints: id and age are integers and never null
first and last are text values copied as they are
Every input row appears once in the output
reference:
SELECT
  id AS student_id,
  first AS first_name,
  last AS last_name,
  age AS age_in_years
FROM students;
brute:
WITH renamed (student_id, first_name, last_name, age_in_years) AS (
  SELECT id, first, last, age FROM students
)
SELECT student_id, first_name, last_name, age_in_years
FROM renamed
notes:
## Intuition

pandas renames columns with `students.rename(columns={...})`. A SQL query never changes a stored table here; instead, the name of each output column is whatever the `SELECT` list calls it. Giving every column an alias with `AS` produces exactly the renamed table, row for row.

## Approach

1. List the four columns in their original order.
2. Give each one its new name: `id AS student_id`, `first AS first_name`, `last AS last_name`, `age AS age_in_years`.
3. Read `FROM students` with no `WHERE`, so every row, duplicates included, comes through unchanged.

## Example 1, step by step

- Row `(1, Mason, King, 6)` comes out as `student_id = 1`, `first_name = Mason`, `last_name = King`, `age_in_years = 6`.
- The same happens to Ava Wright (2, 7), Taylor Hall (3, 16), Georgia Thompson (4, 18) and Thomas Moore (5, 10).

Only the header changes; all five rows keep their values.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n) for n rows; each row is copied once.
- Space: O(n) for the output.

## Pitfalls

- A misspelled or missing alias (`age_years`, or no `AS` at all) leaves the wrong header, and the result is judged on column names too.
- Swapping two aliases (`first AS last_name`) keeps the right headers but puts the wrong values under them.
- `SELECT DISTINCT` would merge duplicate rows; renaming must keep every row.

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `students` | the input table, every row kept |
| `student_id` | the new name of `id` |
| `first_name`, `last_name` | the new names of `first` and `last` |
| `age_in_years` | the new name of `age` |

narration.1: Each output row is one input row; only the column names change.
narration.2: Rename id to student_id with an alias.
narration.6: Read every row of students with no filter.
